title: Panama Separates from Colombia with US Backing
description: On November 3, 1903, Panama declared independence from Colombia following a US-backed revolt, with the USS Nashville blocking Colombian troops from suppressing the secession. The United States recognized the new republic within three days. The separation was directly engineered to secure American rights to build a canal across the isthmus.

title: Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty Grants US Canal Zone
description: The new Panamanian government signed the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty in November 1903, granting the United States perpetual control over a ten-mile-wide Canal Zone across the isthmus in exchange for $10 million and annual payments. The treaty was negotiated by a French citizen acting as Panama's minister without the Panamanian delegation present. The deeply unequal agreement would fuel nationalist resentment for the next seven decades.

title: Panama's First Constitution Establishes Republic
description: Panama adopted its first constitution on February 13, 1904, establishing a republican government modeled partly on US institutions. The constitution included a provision allowing the United States to intervene to maintain order, reflecting the new nation's dependent relationship with Washington. The founding document also established the abolition of the army.

title: US Canal Construction Begins under Colonel Gorgas
description: The United States took over canal construction in 1904 under the Isthmian Canal Commission, with Colonel William Gorgas leading a public health campaign to eradicate yellow fever and malaria that had defeated earlier French efforts. The sanitation program dramatically reduced disease mortality among workers and residents. Construction of one of the world's greatest engineering projects formally commenced.

title: Miraflores and Pedro Miguel Locks Construction Advances
description: Canal construction progressed significantly through 1908 with the excavation of the Culebra Cut through the continental divide and construction of the major lock chambers. The workforce at its peak exceeded 40,000 workers, primarily from the Caribbean islands, Europe, and the United States. Labor conditions were segregated, with West Indian workers receiving lower pay and poorer housing than white American workers.

title: Panama Canal Opens to Commercial Traffic
description: The Panama Canal opened on August 15, 1914, when the cargo ship SS Ancon made the first official transit through the completed waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. The 77-kilometer canal immediately transformed global maritime trade by eliminating the need to navigate around Cape Horn. The US-controlled Canal Zone became a state within a state, generating ongoing tensions with Panamanian sovereignty.

title: Kuna Rebellion Establishes Indigenous Autonomy
description: The Kuna (Guna) people of the San Blas archipelago launched the Tule Revolt in February 1925 against Panamanian government efforts to suppress their traditional culture and governance. With tacit US support, the revolt succeeded in negotiating the Kuna's recognition as a semi-autonomous people. The Comarca Kuna Yala established a precedent for indigenous self-governance in Panama.

title: Accion Comunal Coup Ends Oligarchic Political Order
description: A nationalist movement called Accion Comunal staged a successful coup on January 2, 1931, overthrowing President Florencio Harmodio Arosemena and marking the end of Panama's founding oligarchic political families' unchallenged dominance. The coup represented the first interruption of constitutional government and the emergence of middle-class and popular political forces. It signaled rising Panamanian nationalism against both the traditional elite and US influence.

title: Hull-Alfaro Treaty Revises Canal Agreement
description: Panama and the United States signed the Hull-Alfaro Treaty, renegotiating the 1903 treaty to increase Panama's annuity from the Canal Zone, eliminate the US right of intervention in Panamanian affairs, and grant Panamanians somewhat better access to Canal Zone commerce. The treaty was a partial concession to growing Panamanian nationalism. It represented the first significant revision of the unequal 1903 arrangement.

title: President Arias Ousted After Refusing US Bases
description: Arnulfo Arias, Panama's populist and nationalist president, was overthrown in October 1941 by a US-backed coup after he refused to grant additional military base rights during World War II and adopted a new constitution that restricted citizenship rights of non-Spanish-speaking immigrants. Arias's removal demonstrated the United States' willingness to topple Panamanian governments that challenged its strategic interests. He would return to politics repeatedly over the next four decades.

title: National Assembly Rejects US Base Rights Agreement
description: Panama's National Assembly unanimously rejected a proposed defense sites agreement that would have allowed the United States to retain 134 military bases and installations after World War II. The rejection followed massive popular demonstrations in Panama City led by students and nationalists. The episode signaled a new assertiveness in Panamanian sovereignty politics.

title: Colonel Jose Antonio Remon Elected President
description: Colonel Jose Antonio Remon Cantera, commander of the National Police, won the 1952 presidential election, marking the formal entry of the security forces into direct political control. Remon negotiated a new canal treaty with Washington and modernized Panama's National Guard. His presidency established the institutional pattern of military influence over Panamanian politics that would persist for decades.

title: Remon-Eisenhower Treaty Increases Canal Payments
description: Panama and the United States signed the Remon-Eisenhower Treaty in January 1955, increasing the Canal Zone annuity from $430,000 to $1.93 million and granting Panamanians fairer access to commercial opportunities in the Zone. President Remon was assassinated before ratification, in January 1955, in a killing whose perpetrators remained a subject of controversy. The treaty represented modest progress on Panamanian demands for a fairer share of canal revenues.

title: Flag Riots Precede 1964: First Major Canal Protest
description: Panamanian students attempted to plant the Panamanian flag in the Canal Zone in November 1959, triggering clashes with Canal Zone police and US soldiers that left dozens injured. The riots revealed the explosive potential of the flag and sovereignty issue. The Eisenhower administration responded by agreeing that Panama's flag could be flown alongside the US flag at one location in the Zone.

title: Flag Riots Kill 21 Panamanians; Diplomatic Rupture with US
description: On January 9, 1964, Panamanian students attempted to march through the Canal Zone carrying their national flag, triggering violent clashes in which US soldiers and Zonians killed 21 Panamanians and wounded hundreds. Panama broke diplomatic relations with the United States and the incident became a defining moment of Panamanian nationalism. The riots ultimately forced US acceptance that the 1903 treaty had to be fundamentally renegotiated.

title: Panama Brings Canal Sovereignty Dispute to OAS
description: Following the Flag Riots, Panama brought its case to the Organization of American States and the United Nations, winning broad international sympathy for its position that the 1903 treaty was inequitable and should be renegotiated. The United States agreed to open negotiations on a new treaty framework. The international pressure campaign represented Panama's successful use of multilateral diplomacy to confront a much more powerful adversary.

title: General Omar Torrijos Seizes Power in Military Coup
description: General Omar Torrijos Herrera led a National Guard coup on October 11, 1968, ousting the newly elected president Arnulfo Arias just eleven days into his third term. Torrijos established himself as Maximum Leader of the Panamanian Revolution without assuming the presidency, ruling through allied civilian presidents while retaining real power through the military. His government combined nationalism, social reformism, and authoritarianism in a style that defied Cold War categorization.

title: New Constitution Formalizes Torrijos's Power
description: A new constitution enacted in 1972 institutionalized Torrijos's authority by creating the position of Maximum Leader of the Panamanian Revolution, giving him supreme executive power for six years while maintaining civilian presidents as figureheads. The constitution also expanded social rights and codified the nationalist agenda. Torrijos used this period to pursue the Canal treaty negotiations that would become his defining legacy.

title: Torrijos-Carter Treaties Agree to Return Canal by 1999
description: US President Jimmy Carter and General Omar Torrijos signed two treaties in Washington on September 7, 1977, agreeing to transfer sovereignty of the Panama Canal to Panama by December 31, 1999, and guaranteeing Panama's permanent neutrality. The treaties passed a narrow US Senate ratification and were celebrated across Panama and Latin America. They represented the most significant US concession on Cold War-era hemisphere relations and Torrijos's greatest political achievement.

title: Panama Ratifies Canal Treaties in National Plebiscite
description: Panamanian voters approved the Torrijos-Carter Treaties in a national plebiscite with a two-thirds majority, despite opposition from Arnulfo Arias loyalists who argued the terms were insufficient. The treaties created a transition period of joint administration leading to full Panamanian control in 1999. Ratification launched two decades of preparations for Panamanian operation of the waterway.

title: General Torrijos Dies in Suspicious Plane Crash
description: General Omar Torrijos was killed when his small plane crashed on July 31, 1981, in the mountains of Cocle province, with all aboard dying in the crash. The cause was officially declared an accident, but persistent allegations of sabotage — including speculation of CIA involvement — were never definitively resolved. Torrijos's death created a power vacuum that ultimately led to the rise of Manuel Noriega.

title: General Manuel Noriega Takes Control of National Defense Forces
description: Manuel Antonio Noriega consolidated control of Panama's military as commander of the National Defense Forces in 1983 following a period of succession struggles after Torrijos's death. Noriega had long-standing relationships with both the CIA and Cuban intelligence, making him a central figure in Cold War covert operations in Central America. He proceeded to dominate Panamanian politics through manipulation of elections and political terror.

title: Noriega Rigs Presidential Election for Barletta
description: The 1984 presidential election was openly fraudulent, with Noriega's military annulling ballot returns and falsifying results to install Nicolas Ardito Barletta over the popular Arnulfo Arias by fewer than 2,000 votes. The fraud was reported by international observers and acknowledged by US officials who nevertheless recognized the result for geopolitical reasons. The stolen election demonstrated the military's complete dominance over Panamanian democracy.

title: Hugo Spadafora Tortured and Beheaded by Noriega Forces
description: Hugo Spadafora, a critic and former Torrijos loyalist who claimed to have evidence of Noriega's drug trafficking, was found decapitated in Costa Rica on September 14, 1985, after Panamanian authorities detained him at the border. The brutal murder shocked Panama and generated the first sustained organized opposition to Noriega's regime. No one was ever convicted, but the killing was widely attributed to Noriega's direct order.

title: Colonel Diaz Herrera Accusations Trigger Civic Crusade
description: Retired colonel Roberto Diaz Herrera publicly accused Noriega of ordering Spadafora's murder, rigging the 1984 election, and involvement in Torrijos's death in June 1987. The allegations sparked the formation of the Civic Crusade, a broad opposition coalition of business, professional, and civil society groups that organized massive demonstrations. The Noriega regime responded with tear gas, beatings, and arrest of demonstrators.

title: US Indicts Noriega on Drug Trafficking Charges
description: US federal grand juries in Miami and Tampa indicted General Manuel Noriega in February 1988 on charges of drug trafficking and money laundering, alleging he had accepted millions from the Medellin Cartel to allow cocaine shipments through Panama. The indictments transformed the bilateral relationship and made the personal removal of Noriega a US policy objective. Subsequent economic sanctions caused severe damage to the Panamanian economy.

title: Opposition Wins Election; Noriega Annuls and Beats Candidates
description: The May 1989 presidential election saw the opposition ticket of Guillermo Endara, Ricardo Arias Calderon, and Guillermo Ford win by a large margin confirmed by independent observers including former US President Carter. Noriega annulled the results and had regime thugs beat the opposition candidates in public, the images broadcast worldwide. Endara, Ford, and Calderon received severe beatings that became iconic photographs of Noriega's brutality.

title: Operation Just Cause: US Invades Panama and Removes Noriega
description: On December 20, 1989, the United States launched Operation Just Cause, deploying approximately 27,000 troops in the largest US military operation since Vietnam to remove Manuel Noriega from power. The invasion killed an estimated 300-500 Panamanian civilians and soldiers along with 23 American soldiers, and destroyed the El Chorrillo neighborhood of Panama City. Noriega took refuge in the Vatican nunciature before surrendering to US forces on January 3, 1990.

title: Endara Government Inaugurated; Panama Abolishes Military
description: Guillermo Endara, the legitimately elected 1989 winner, was sworn in as president on a US military base as Operation Just Cause began, and his government was recognized internationally. Panama permanently abolished its military in 1990 and converted the National Defense Forces into a civilian police force. The abolition of the armed forces was enshrined in a 1994 constitutional amendment, establishing Panama as one of the few countries without a standing army.

title: El Chorrillo Reconstruction and Post-Invasion Recovery
description: The El Chorrillo neighborhood of Panama City was largely destroyed during Operation Just Cause, leaving thousands of residents homeless. The post-invasion recovery was complicated by US promises of $1 billion in aid that were partially delayed by congressional opposition. The physical and economic reconstruction of Panama took several years and the invasion's legacy remained deeply contested.

title: Noriega Convicted on Drug Trafficking in Miami
description: Manuel Noriega was tried in a Miami federal court and convicted in April 1992 on eight counts of drug trafficking, racketeering, and money laundering, receiving a 40-year sentence that was later reduced. The trial was the first in US history where a foreign head of state was prosecuted on criminal charges. Noriega subsequently served sentences in the United States, France, and Panama before his death in 2017.

title: Ernesto Perez Balladares Elected; Military Abolition Enshrined
description: Ernesto Perez Balladares of the Democratic Revolutionary Party (the former Noriega party, rebranded) won the 1994 presidential election in a fragmented field, beginning a period of democratic consolidation. The same year, Panama constitutionally enshrined the prohibition of a standing army. The election demonstrated that Panama's democratic transition was stabilizing following the turbulent Noriega era.

title: Panama Canal Authority Established for Transition
description: The Panamanian government created the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) in 1994 to prepare for the 1999 handover, establishing a merit-based management structure modeled on best practices in the shipping industry. Panamanian engineers, administrators, and pilots began intensive training to operate the canal. The transition planning period was widely credited with ensuring an operationally seamless handover.

title: Mireya Moscoso Runs for President; Arnulfista Party Surges
description: Mireya Moscoso, widow of three-time president Arnulfo Arias and leader of the Arnulfista Party, mounted a strong presidential campaign that energized the Panamanian right. Her campaign focused on canal handover sovereignty concerns and anti-corruption. She narrowly lost to Perez Balladares in a sign of a competitive emerging democracy.

title: Hurricane Mitch Spares Panama but Devastates Neighbors
description: Hurricane Mitch, one of the deadliest Atlantic hurricanes on record, caused catastrophic destruction in Honduras, Nicaragua, and Guatemala in October 1998 while causing significantly less damage in Panama. The disaster intensified Central American migration northward and created regional humanitarian challenges. Panama provided transit assistance and some aid to neighboring countries' recovery efforts.

title: Mireya Moscoso Elected First Female President
description: Mireya Moscoso won the May 1999 presidential election, becoming Panama's first female president and defeating the PRD candidate Martin Torrijos. Her election year coincided with the canal handover, making it a doubly historic moment. Moscoso's administration was marked by the triumphant canal transfer but also significant corruption scandals.

title: Panama Takes Full Control of the Canal
description: On December 31, 1999, at noon, the United States formally transferred full sovereignty and operational control of the Panama Canal to Panama, fulfilling the 1977 Torrijos-Carter Treaties. President Mireya Moscoso received the canal in a ceremony attended by former US President Carter. The handover ended nearly a century of US control and was celebrated as a defining moment of Panamanian nationhood.

title: US Forces Depart; Former Canal Zone Redeveloped
description: The final US military forces withdrew from Panama on December 31, 1999, ending US military presence that had existed since 1903. The former Canal Zone containing US military bases and installations was transferred to Panama, presenting a massive economic development opportunity. Panama subsequently redeveloped the former zone into commercial, residential, and educational facilities, including the City of Knowledge research park.

title: Panama Refuses to Join US Coalition in Iraq War
description: Panama declined to join the US-led coalition of forces invading Iraq in 2003, citing its constitutional prohibition on military forces and its traditional policy of neutrality. The decision reflected Panama's genuine pacifist tradition rather than anti-Americanism. Panama maintained close economic and diplomatic ties with Washington while asserting an independent foreign policy on military matters.

title: Martin Torrijos Elected; Canal Expansion Planned
description: Martin Torrijos, son of General Omar Torrijos, won the 2004 presidential election on a platform of economic development and canal expansion. His government launched the planning process for the Third Set of Locks project to expand canal capacity. The election continued the pattern of alternation between Panama's two main political blocs.

title: Panama Votes to Expand the Canal
description: Panamanian voters approved the $5.25 billion Panama Canal Expansion Project by 76.8% in a national referendum on October 22, 2006. The project involved building a new set of larger locks on both the Atlantic and Pacific sides to accommodate Post-Panamax container ships. The expansion, completed in 2016, doubled the canal's capacity and transformed its competitive position in global shipping.

title: Canal Expansion Construction Begins
description: The Panama Canal expansion project officially broke ground in September 2007, beginning one of the largest infrastructure projects in the Western Hemisphere since the original canal construction. International consortia including Spanish, Italian, Belgian, and Panamanian companies competed for major contracts. The project employed tens of thousands of workers over nearly a decade of construction.

title: Global Financial Crisis Slows Panama's Economy
description: The 2008-2009 global financial crisis slowed Panama's economy though far less severely than most countries, as strong canal revenues and service exports provided relative resilience. Canal traffic volumes declined modestly but Panama's dollarized economy and fiscal reserves cushioned the impact. The crisis underscored Panama's dependence on global trade flows while demonstrating the canal's stabilizing role.

title: Ricardo Martinelli Wins Presidency on Anti-Corruption Platform
description: Ricardo Martinelli, a supermarket magnate and leader of the conservative Democratic Change party, won the May 2009 presidential election with nearly 60% of the vote on a populist anti-corruption platform. Martinelli's outsider campaign capitalized on public frustration with established political parties. His government initially achieved strong economic growth but was later marred by serious corruption scandals and abuse of power allegations.

title: Panama Removed from FATF Gray List
description: The Financial Action Task Force removed Panama from its list of countries with strategic anti-money-laundering deficiencies in 2010 following legislative reforms. The delisting improved Panama's international financial standing and reputation. However, the offshore financial sector's opacity would continue to generate international scrutiny.

title: Panama among Fastest Growing Economies in Latin America
description: Panama's GDP grew at approximately 10.6% in 2011, making it one of the fastest-growing economies in Latin America, driven by canal expansion construction, financial services, real estate, and logistics. Panama City was experiencing a construction and investment boom with skyline transformation. The strong growth attracted significant foreign direct investment and deepened Panama's role as a regional services hub.

title: Martinelli Surveillance Scandal Revealed
description: Investigations revealed that President Martinelli had used state intelligence resources to conduct illegal surveillance of opposition politicians, journalists, and business rivals using a government spy program. The scandal prompted significant political backlash and judicial investigations. Martinelli denied the allegations but the evidence of systematic wiretapping damaged his administration's credibility.

title: Colon Free Trade Zone Protests Turn Deadly
description: Protests erupted in the Colon Free Trade Zone in October 2012 against government land sales that residents feared would displace the zone's workers and communities. Security forces responded with force, killing at least two protesters and wounding dozens. The violence in Colon, Panama's predominantly Afro-Panamanian Caribbean port city, drew attention to longstanding inequality between the capital and provinces.

title: Juan Carlos Varela Wins Presidency; Martinelli Faces Prosecution
description: Juan Carlos Varela, a former Martinelli ally turned rival, won the May 2014 presidential election, defeating Martinelli's chosen successor Jose Domingo Arias. Varela immediately faced accusations that Martinelli had conducted illegal wiretapping of his communications during the campaign. Martinelli subsequently fled to the United States ahead of corruption investigations in Panama.

title: Panama Papers Expose Global Offshore Financial System
description: On April 3, 2016, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists published the Panama Papers, 11.5 million leaked documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca revealing the offshore financial arrangements of 12 current and former heads of state, 128 other politicians and officials, and thousands of wealthy individuals from 200 countries. The leak was the largest in journalistic history at that time. Panama's name became globally synonymous with tax avoidance and financial secrecy despite most of the beneficiaries being foreigners.

title: Panama Canal Expanded with New Third Set of Locks
description: The expanded Panama Canal, featuring a new third lane of larger neo-Panamax locks, was officially inaugurated on June 26, 2016, in a ceremony attended by heads of state and global shipping executives. The expansion allowed the passage of vessels carrying three times the cargo of the largest ships that could previously transit. The project was completed substantially on schedule despite labor disputes and cost overruns.

title: Panama and Colombia Open Colon-Bogota Highway Link
description: Infrastructure connectivity in the region advanced with new road and development corridor projects linking Panama City to the Colombian border, facilitating regional trade. The Darien Gap remained the only break in the Pan-American Highway, but logistics infrastructure on both sides improved. Regional integration through physical connectivity became a development priority.

title: Panama Establishes Diplomatic Relations with China
description: Panama announced on June 12, 2017, that it was switching diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to the People's Republic of China, becoming the largest Central American economy and the first country with close ties to the Panama Canal to recognize Beijing. The decision was driven by substantial Chinese shipping interests in the canal and promises of significant Chinese investment. The move was seen as a major Chinese diplomatic victory and significant blow to Taiwan's regional standing.

title: Laurentino Cortizo Wins Presidency; Anti-Corruption Agenda
description: Laurentino 'Nito' Cortizo of the Democratic Revolutionary Party won the May 2019 presidential election by a narrow margin over former government minister Romulo Roux, campaigning on anti-corruption and economic revival themes. His government faced immediate challenges from the Panama Papers legacy and the Odebrecht construction bribery scandal that implicated Panamanian officials. The election demonstrated continued voter demand for accountability.

title: Martinelli Extradited from US to Face Trial in Panama
description: Former president Ricardo Martinelli was extradited from the United States to Panama in June 2018 to face trial on charges of illegal wiretapping and corruption. Martinelli had previously sought asylum in the US, where he had fled in 2015, but a US judge ordered his extradition after rejecting asylum claims. His return to face justice was seen as an important test of Panama's rule of law.

title: Odebrecht Bribery Scandal Implicates Panamanian Officials
description: Investigations into the Brazilian construction giant Odebrecht's regional bribery scheme implicated several Panamanian officials and former presidents in payments related to major infrastructure contracts. The scandal was part of a continent-wide corruption investigation that had already toppled governments in Brazil, Peru, and other countries. Panama's attorney general's office pursued multiple cases, though prosecutions proceeded slowly.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic: Panama Imposes Strict Gendered Lockdown
description: Panama recorded its first COVID-19 cases in March 2020 and imposed one of Latin America's strictest lockdowns, including an unusual gendered quarantine system allowing men and women to leave home on alternate days. The country suffered high per-capita mortality partly due to pre-existing socioeconomic inequalities. Economic contraction exceeded 17% in 2020, the deepest recession in Panama's modern history.

title: Panama Returns to FATF Gray List on Money Laundering
description: The Financial Action Task Force placed Panama back on its gray list of countries under increased monitoring for deficiencies in combating money laundering and terrorist financing. The relisting damaged Panama's reputation as a financial center and increased compliance burdens on financial institutions. It reflected persistent challenges in regulating the offshore financial sector despite post-Panama Papers reforms.

title: Darien Gap Migration Surge Reaches Record Levels
description: Migrants crossing the dangerous Darien Gap jungle between Colombia and Panama reached record numbers in 2021, with over 133,000 people making the crossing — more than in any previous year. The migrants included Haitians, Venezuelans, Cubans, and people from Africa and Asia attempting to reach the United States. Panama was overwhelmed by the humanitarian challenge of processing and transiting hundreds of thousands of migrants through its territory.

title: Drought Reduces Canal Water Levels; Traffic Restrictions
description: Severe drought conditions reduced water levels in Gatun Lake, the artificial lake that feeds the canal's locks, to historically low levels, forcing the Panama Canal Authority to restrict the draft of vessels using the waterway. The restrictions forced shipping companies to carry lighter loads or use alternative routes, causing significant economic disruption to global supply chains. The drought highlighted climate change as an existential threat to canal operations.

title: Martinelli Convicted of Money Laundering
description: Former president Ricardo Martinelli was convicted in Panama by a court on money laundering charges related to the purchase of a media company with alleged illicit funds in a case that had taken over a decade to prosecute. The conviction was a significant milestone for Panamanian accountability but Martinelli continued to face multiple other legal proceedings. He was also elected to the National Assembly from prison, creating a constitutional controversy over legislative immunity.

title: Cobre Panama Copper Mine Protests Force Closure
description: Massive nationwide protests erupted in October-November 2023 against the government's contract renewal with First Quantum Minerals for the Cobre Panama copper mine, one of the world's largest open-pit mines. Demonstrators blocked the Pan-American Highway and the canal access roads for weeks, citing environmental concerns and the lack of public consultation. President Cortizo ordered the mine shut down and a Supreme Court ruling declared the contract unconstitutional, forcing the mine's closure with enormous economic consequences.

title: Canal Drought Reaches Crisis Level; Vessel Backlogs
description: Gatun Lake water levels fell to historic lows in late 2023 due to a severe El Nino-intensified drought, forcing the Panama Canal Authority to reduce daily transits from 36-38 to fewer than 24 ships. Hundreds of vessels queued for weeks at both entrances to the canal, with waiting times exceeding three weeks for some ship categories. The crisis caused estimated billions in additional shipping costs and prompted warnings about climate change's long-term threat to canal viability.

title: Jose Raul Mulino Wins Presidency Amid Martinelli Drama
description: Jose Raul Mulino, a former security minister who had been Martinelli's running mate before the Supreme Court disqualified Martinelli from running, won the May 2024 presidential election with approximately 34% of the vote in a fragmented field. His victory followed a campaign in which Martinelli received asylum in Nicaragua after fleeing the Panamanian nunciature. Mulino's government faced immediate challenges including the Cobre Panama mine closure, migration pressure, and economic uncertainty.

title: Darien Gap Crossings Exceed 500,000 in Single Year
description: Over half a million migrants crossed the Darien Gap in 2024, making it by far the largest crossing in recorded history, driven by migration from Venezuela, Ecuador, Haiti, and increasingly from outside the Americas. The Mulino government attempted to introduce restrictions and deportation agreements with the United States and countries of origin. The humanitarian situation in the Darien jungle reception camps remained dire with significant deaths and violence.

title: Panama Qualifies for Its First-Ever FIFA World Cup
description: On October 10, 2017, Panama secured its first-ever World Cup berth with an 88th-minute goal from Roman Torres in a 2-1 win over Costa Rica in the final round of CONCACAF qualifying, a result that also eliminated the United States from qualification. President Juan Carlos Varela declared a national holiday the following day to celebrate the achievement. Panama went on to play its first World Cup match at Russia 2018, with Felipe Baloy scoring the country's first-ever World Cup goal.
